---
name: experiment3-iter0-critique-stats
description: exp3 iter_0 critique of uncertainty_shifted_criterion — data structure + 8 PPC stats with observed values
metadata:
  type: project
---
Exp3 data (2026-10-31): 15 participants × 450 trials (split on trial_index==0), 6750 rows, ~190 sets, adaptive-looking design (5–270 trials per set). Participant yes rates fall in three blocks of 5 (≈0.40, 0.58, 0.49). Very noisy: shown-example targets only 66% yes, and many sets sit near 0.5. No MCMC cache existed at critique time.
iter_0 stats, observed: participant_yes_rate_sd 0.071; participant_parity_discrimination_sd 0.16; parity_span_interaction -0.065; lag1_response_repeat 0.539; single_example_distance_gradient (≤10 vs ≥40) 0.02; setsize_outspan_sharpening (n4−n2) 0.012; shown_example_target_yes 0.658; multiple_rule_vs_span_preference (k 3..12) 0.27.
**Why:** so later rounds don't probe the same things again; exp2 versions of lag1/participant SD/target-in-set were null ([[experiment2-iter4-critique-stats]]).
**How to apply:** read iter_0/critique/ppc_results.json for hits before choosing iter_1 stats.
---
name: experiment3-iter1-critique-stats
description: exp3 iter_1 critique of kind_uncertainty_shifted_criterion — 8 new PPC stats + observed values; numpy MAP refit script for residual scans
metadata:
  type: project
---
iter_1 critique (2026-10-31), incumbent kind_uncertainty_shifted_criterion (iter_0 got 0/8; closest multiple_rule_vs_span_preference p=0.08).
New stats, observed (rough binomial null from a numpy MAP refit, ignoring posterior spread): decade_shared_contrast -0.062 (null -0.040, z≈-2); target_100_yes 0.46 (null 0.39, z≈1.9); participant_set_consistency 0.258 (null 0.265, z≈-1.5, people LESS consistent within a set than the model); prime_set_two_target 0.08; rule_set_member_far_outspan 0.73; odd_set_even_target_yes 0.58; single_example_multiple_yes -0.01; late_session_yes_drop -0.07.
Model fits marginals (set size, span, parity, blocks, halves) almost exactly; residuals look like noise.
Refit script: /tmp/crit3/fit.py (Powell over lam, mean_share, conc, 8 family logits, shift; ll -3646 in ~min) writes per-row p to /tmp/crit3/pred.csv; /tmp/crit3/sim.py <stat files> gives quick z.
**Why:** avoid re-probing; see [[experiment3-iter0-critique-stats]].
**How to apply:** read iter_1/critique/ppc_results.json for hits before choosing iter_2 stats.
---
name: experiment3-iter2-critique-stats
description: exp3 iter_2 critique of kind_uncertainty_shifted_criterion — 8 new PPC stats + observed values (iter_1 got 0/8)
metadata:
  type: project
---
iter_2 critique (2026-10-31), incumbent still kind_uncertainty_shifted_criterion; iter_1 had 0/8 hits (closest decade_shared_contrast p=0.08, target_100_yes p=0.10).
New stats, observed: near_outspan_generalization (1-5 outside span, n>=2) 0.380; units_digit_shared_contrast -0.019; powers2_set_even_nonpower_yes 0.315; prime_set_prime_vs_odd_composite 0.195; set_yes_rate_sd (sets >=20 trials) 0.242; small_vs_large_target_contrast (<=10 vs >=91) 0.032; round_target_yes_nonround_sets -0.045; wide_sparse_interior_yes (n>=3, span>=30) 0.481.
Committed from reasoning only, with no null simulation run.
**Why:** so later rounds don't probe these again; see [[experiment3-iter1-critique-stats]].
**How to apply:** read iter_2/critique/ppc_results.json for hits before choosing iter_3 stats.

"""Refinement of `kind_uncertainty_shifted_criterion`: people infer the hidden
concept as its Bayesian concept learner does (45 rules with a family-organised
prior and exception rules as their own family, all intervals of 1..100 with a
beta prior over the share of the line a range covers, size principle with 90%
of examples drawn from the concept), and their yes/no criterion shifts with
doubt about what kind of program they face. The one change is which part of
that doubt counts: the incumbent's kind entropy splits exactly into
rule-versus-range doubt plus P(rule) times the doubt among rule families given
a rule; only the second part (doubt about which kind of arithmetic rule,
weighted by belief that it is a rule) shifts the criterion here.
"""

import numpy as np
import pymc as pm
import pytensor.tensor as pt
from scipy.special import logsumexp

ALPHA = 0.9
NUMBERS = np.arange(1, 101)


def rule_concepts():
    rules = {
        "odd": [n for n in NUMBERS if n % 2 == 1],
        "primes": [n for n in NUMBERS if n > 1 and all(n % a for a in range(2, int(n**0.5) + 1))],
        "squares": [n * n for n in range(1, 11)],
        "cubes": [n**3 for n in range(1, 5)],
        "powers of 2, not 32": [2, 4, 8, 16, 64],
        "powers of 2, or 37": [2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 37, 64],
        "even": list(range(2, 101, 2)),
    }
    rules.update({f"multiples of {m}": list(range(m, 101, m)) for m in [3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 11, 12]})
    rules.update({f"powers of {m}": [m**k for k in range(1, 8) if m**k <= 100] for m in range(2, 11)})
    rules.update({f"ends in {d}": [n for n in NUMBERS if n % 10 == d] for d in range(10)})
    rules.update({f"contains digit {d}": [n for n in NUMBERS if str(d) in str(n)] for d in range(10)})
    return rules


_RULES = rule_concepts()
RULE_NAMES, RULES = list(_RULES), list(_RULES.values())
N_RULES = len(RULES)
INTERVALS = [list(range(m, n + 1)) for m in NUMBERS for n in range(m, 101)]
MEMBERSHIP = np.array([np.isin(NUMBERS, c) for c in RULES + INTERVALS], dtype="float64")
EXAMPLE_LOG_LIK = np.log(ALPHA * MEMBERSHIP / MEMBERSHIP.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True) + (1 - ALPHA) / 100)
RULE_MEMBERSHIP = MEMBERSHIP[:N_RULES]
INTERVAL_MEMBERSHIP = MEMBERSHIP[N_RULES:]
INTERVAL_SIZE_IDX = (INTERVAL_MEMBERSHIP.sum(axis=1) - 1).astype("int64")  # L - 1
SIZES = np.arange(1, 101, dtype="float64")
LOG_N_OF_SIZE = np.log(101.0 - SIZES)  # number of intervals of each size
SHARE = (SIZES - 0.5) / 100.0  # share of the 1..100 line covered, in (0, 1)

def rule_family(name):
    if name in ("odd", "even"):
        return 0
    if name == "primes":
        return 1
    if name in ("squares", "cubes"):
        return 2
    if name.startswith("powers of 2,"):
        return 7
    if name.startswith("powers"):
        return 3
    if name.startswith("multiples"):
        return 4
    if name.startswith("ends in"):
        return 5
    return 6


FAMILY = np.array([rule_family(n) for n in RULE_NAMES])
N_FAMILIES = FAMILY.max() + 1
FAMILY_SIZE = np.bincount(FAMILY)

# All intervals of one size share their prior, so prepare_observed sums each
# set's interval likelihood within every size (parameter-free) and records, per
# size, the share of that evidence from intervals containing each target.

with pm.Model() as model:
    rule_log_lik = pm.Data("rule_log_lik", np.zeros((1, N_RULES)))  # (sets, rules)
    size_log_evidence = pm.Data("size_log_evidence", np.zeros((1, 100)))  # (sets, sizes): log sum_j P(D|j)

# name: digit_reversal_target_contrast
# description: Yes rate for targets that are the digit reversal of a shown two-digit example (e.g. 38 for 83; target not itself shown) minus the mean yes rate of that set's other targets; observed below null means people reject reversals more than the model's shared-digit rules predict, above means they treat reversals as same-concept.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric).to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    y = df["rating"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    valid = ~np.isnan(ex)
    e = np.nan_to_num(ex).astype(int)
    tens, units = e // 10, e % 10
    revable = valid & (e >= 10) & (e <= 99) & (units != 0) & (tens != units)
    rev = units * 10 + tens
    is_rev = (revable & (rev == t[:, None])).any(axis=1)
    shown = (valid & (e == t[:, None])).any(axis=1)
    is_rev &= ~shown
    sets = df["number_set"].to_numpy()
    s = pd.Series(y)
    g = pd.DataFrame({"set": sets, "y": y, "r": is_rev})
    tot = g.groupby("set")["y"].transform("sum")
    cnt = g.groupby("set")["y"].transform("count")
    other_mean = (tot - g["y"]) / np.maximum(cnt - 1, 1)
    if is_rev.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(np.mean(y[is_rev] - other_mean.to_numpy()[is_rev]))
EOF
cat << 'EOF' > double_half_target_contrast.py
# name: double_half_target_contrast
# description: Set-demeaned yes rate for targets equal to twice or half of a shown example, in sets that are not all powers of 2 (target not shown); observed above null means people generalize by doubling/halving relations the model lacks, below means the model over-credits them.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric).to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    y = df["rating"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    valid = ~np.isnan(ex)
    e = np.nan_to_num(ex).astype(int)
    p2 = np.isin(e, [1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64])
    all_p2 = (p2 | ~valid).all(axis=1)
    rel = valid & ((2 * e == t[:, None]) | ((e % 2 == 0) & (e // 2 == t[:, None])))
    shown = (valid & (e == t[:, None])).any(axis=1)
    flag = rel.any(axis=1) & ~shown & ~all_p2
    g = pd.DataFrame({"set": df["number_set"].to_numpy(), "y": y})
    tot = g.groupby("set")["y"].transform("sum").to_numpy()
    cnt = g.groupby("set")["y"].transform("count").to_numpy()
    other = (tot - y) / np.maximum(cnt - 1, 1)
    if flag.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(np.mean(y[flag] - other[flag]))
EOF
cat << 'EOF' > below_vs_above_span_asymmetry.py
# name: below_vs_above_span_asymmetry
# description: For sets of >=2 examples, yes rate for targets 1-15 below the smallest example minus yes rate for targets 1-15 above the largest; the model's ranges are symmetric, so observed above (below) null means people extend concepts downward (upward) more than predicted.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric).to_numpy(dtype=float)
    n = (~np.isnan(ex)).sum(axis=1)
    lo, hi = np.nanmin(ex, axis=1), np.nanmax(ex, axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    y = df["rating"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    below = (n >= 2) & (t < lo) & (lo - t <= 15)
    above = (n >= 2) & (t > hi) & (t - hi <= 15)
    if below.sum() == 0 or above.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(y[below].mean() - y[above].mean())
EOF
cat << 'EOF' > recency_endpoint_proximity.py
# name: recency_endpoint_proximity
# description: Among targets 1-20 outside the span of a >=2-example set, yes rate when the nearest span endpoint was the last example shown minus when it was the first shown; the model is order-blind, so observed above null means a recency boost in generalization (below means primacy).
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric).to_numpy(dtype=float)
    valid = ~np.isnan(ex)
    n = valid.sum(axis=1)
    lo, hi = np.nanmin(ex, axis=1), np.nanmax(ex, axis=1)
    first = ex[:, 0]
    last = ex[np.arange(len(ex)), np.maximum(n - 1, 0)]
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    y = df["rating"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    below = (t < lo) & (lo - t <= 20)
    above = (t > hi) & (t - hi <= 20)
    endpoint = np.where(below, lo, np.where(above, hi, np.nan))
    ok = (n >= 2) & (below | above)
    is_last = ok & (endpoint == last)
    is_first = ok & (endpoint == first)
    if is_last.sum() == 0 or is_first.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(y[is_last].mean() - y[is_first].mean())
EOF
cat << 'EOF' > within_set_target_profile_sd.py
# name: within_set_target_profile_sd
# description: Mean over sets with >=100 trials of the SD across targets (each with >=5 answers) of target-level yes rates; observed above null means people's generalization profiles within a set are sharper (more all-or-none across targets) than the model's, below means flatter.
def test_statistic(df):
    g = df.groupby(["number_set", "target"])["rating"].agg(["mean", "count"]).reset_index()
    g = g[g["count"] >= 5]
    sz = df.groupby("number_set").size()
    big = sz[sz >= 100].index
    g = g[g["number_set"].isin(big)]
    sds = g.groupby("number_set")["mean"].std().dropna()
    if len(sds) == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(sds.mean())
EOF

# description: For sets spanning >=20, yes rate for unshown targets strictly inside the span with 4 examples minus with 2 examples; observed above null means extra examples fill in the range more than the model's size principle predicts, below means less.
def test_statistic(df):

content.text:
I wrote 8 test statistics to `iter_3/critique/test_stats/`. I ran each one once on the observed data: each returned a finite float in under 0.03 s. I didn't simulate from the model, so I don't know yet whether any of them will show a significant discrepancy.

The previous three rounds found nothing: 0 of 24 statistics were significant. The model already matches the overall patterns (set size, span, parity, participant blocks), so these new ones look for things it either can't represent or treats as symmetric.

| Statistic | What it tests | Observed |
|---|---|---|
| `digit_reversal_target_contrast` | Answers for the digit reversal of a shown example (38 after 83), relative to that set's other targets. The model's shared-digit rules may push these toward yes; people say yes only 31% of the time. | −0.022 |
| `double_half_target_contrast` | Answers for targets that are twice or half a shown example, in sets that aren't powers of 2. The model has no doubling relation. | +0.028 |
| `below_vs_above_span_asymmetry` | Yes rate 1–15 below the smallest example minus 1–15 above the largest. The model's ranges are symmetric. | −0.029 |
| `recency_endpoint_proximity` | Outside the examples' range: yes rate when the nearest example was shown last minus when it was shown first. The model ignores example order. | −0.037 |
| `within_set_target_profile_sd` | How sharp the yes/no pattern across targets is within the large sets. | 0.245 |
| `target_one_yes` | Yes rate for target 1 when 1 wasn't shown (the earlier target-100 statistic came closest, at p=0.10). | 0.39 |
| `interior_yes_setsize_contrast` | Yes rate for targets inside a wide range, 4 examples minus 2: does adding examples fill in a range more than the model predicts? | 0.059 |
| `single_example_unshown_yes` | Overall yes rate after a single example. | 0.442 |

All the larger sets have only about 5 answers per (set, target) pair, so statistics about one specific set would have had little power. All 8 statistics therefore pool across sets. I also saved the observed values to memory so later rounds don't test the same things again.
